intro.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a long ss sound (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.
intro.rule_summary: Learn the letter names, spell names letter by letter, and keep tsch (like English ch) apart from sch (like English sh).

intro.title: Personal pronouns + sein; Ich heiße… / Ich bin… / Ich komme aus…
explanation: Personal pronouns tell us who is speaking or who we are talking about: ich (I), du (you, a friend), er (he), sie (she), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal). The formal Sie always has a capital S.
The verb sein (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist. You use it for names, feelings and states: Ich bin Anna. Ich bin müde.
To say your name you can use heißen: Ich heiße Jonas. To say where you are from, use kommen + aus: Ich komme aus Deutschland.
To say how you feel, do not use 'Ich bin gut'. Say Mir geht es gut. The question is Wie geht es dir?

intro.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age
explanation: Learn 0–12 as separate words: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you say the small number plus -zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn. Watch the changes: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?

intro.title: Regular verbs in the present tense
explanation: German verbs in the dictionary form end in -en: wohnen, lernen, arbeiten, spielen. To use a verb, take off -en. What is left is the stem: wohn-, lern-, arbeit-, spiel-.
Then add an ending that matches the person: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt, wir wohnen, ihr wohnt, sie wohnen. The verb changes, so you always need the right ending.
One present tense is enough: Ich wohne in Berlin means both 'I live in Berlin' and 'I am living in Berlin'.

intro.title: haben, der/die/das, ein/eine and the plural
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The gender is not logical, so always learn a noun together with its article: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch.

intro.title: The verb always comes second
explanation: In a German statement, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject (Ich lerne heute Deutsch.) or something else, such as a time word (Heute lerne ich Deutsch.).
Position 1 can be one word or a short group of words that belong together, for example 'Am Montag' or 'Im Sommer'. Count the whole group as one position. The verb comes right after it.

intro.title: Telling the time, and 'um' and 'am' for when

intro.title: Articles: Nominativ and Akkusativ

intro.title: Modal verbs I: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen
explanation: Modal verbs are small helper verbs that add a meaning to another verb. können = can / to be able to, müssen = must / to have to, wollen = to want to, dürfen = may / to be allowed to. Example: Ich kann Suppe kochen = I can cook soup.

The modal verb is conjugated and stands in second position. The main verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the very end of the sentence: Anna will Tee trinken. In a question the modal verb comes first: Darf ich ein Glas Wasser haben?

Modal verbs are irregular in the singular. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending and are always the same (ich kann, er kann). The vowel often changes in the singular: können → kann, müssen → muss, wollen → will, dürfen → darf. The wir and sie/Sie forms are the same as the infinitive.
When ordering politely, Germans often use möchte (would like) instead of will. Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. sounds friendly, while Ich will einen Kaffee. sounds blunt.

intro.title: Dative articles: dem, der, dem, den
explanation: In German the noun's job in the sentence changes the article. After some small words (prepositions) like mit, bei, von, zu and aus, and after the verb geben (to give) for the person who receives something, you use the dative case.
The dative articles are: masculine dem, feminine der, neuter dem, plural den. Compare: der Verkäufer becomes dem Verkäufer, die Karte becomes der Karte, das Geld becomes dem Geld.
In the plural, the noun usually also gets an -n: die Kinder becomes mit den Kindern. If the plural already ends in -n (die Kunden), nothing is added.
The same pattern works with ein and kein: einem, einer, einem. Some short forms are very common: bei + dem = beim, zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom.
intro.rule_summary: Dative: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, plural die → den (+n); ein → einem, eine → einer; used after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and for the person who receives (geben).

intro.title: Verbs with the dative: helfen, gefallen, gehören, danken
explanation: Most German verbs take an accusative object (Ich sehe dich). intro.title: Possessive articles: mein, dein, sein, ihr
explanation: A possessive article shows who something belongs to: mein Bus (my bus), dein Park (your park). The stem depends on the owner: ich = mein, du = dein, er/es = sein, sie = ihr, wir = unser, ihr = euer, Sie = Ihr.
The ending depends on the noun that follows: its gender, its number and its case. The endings are the same as for ein/eine/ein (and kein): mein Bahnhof, meine Straße, mein Haus, meine Freunde.

In the nominative (the subject) the masculine and neuter forms have no ending. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: Ich sehe meinen Bahnhof. In the dative (after mit, bei, zu, in for where?) the endings are -em, -er, -em, -en: mit meinem Bus, mit meiner Freundin.
In the dative plural the noun also usually gets -n: bei meinen Eltern. Remember: sein = his, ihr = her. The owner decides the stem, not the noun.

intro.title: Pronouns in the accusative and dative: ihn, ihm, mich, mir ...
explanation: When you ask for or give directions, you often talk about people: 'Can you help me?', 'I show you the way', 'I don't see him'. The pronoun changes depending on the verb. With zeigen you have both: the person is dative and the thing is accusative: 'Ich zeige dir den Weg.' Only uns, euch, sie (they) and Sie keep the same form in the accusative as in other cases or the nominative; always check the table.

intro.title: Perfekt with haben: talking about the weekend
explanation: In spoken German you usually talk about the past with the Perfekt. It has two parts: a form of haben (ich habe, du hast, er hat ...) in second position, and the Partizip II (past participle) at the very end of the sentence.

Regular verbs build the Partizip II with ge- + stem + -t: spielen → gespielt, kochen → gekocht. Verbs with a vowel change or other irregularities usually use ge- + stem + -en: sehen → gesehen, schlafen → geschlafen. You have to learn these participles with the verb.
If the stem ends in -t, add -et: arbeiten → gearbeitet. Time words such as am Samstag can start the sentence; haben still stays in second position and the participle stays at the end.

intro.title: Irregular Partizip II: the 40 verbs you need for travel stories
explanation: You already know the Perfekt: a form of haben or sein in second position, and the Partizip II at the end of the sentence. Regular verbs end in -t (gemacht). Many very common verbs are irregular. Their Partizip II usually ends in -en (gesehen, gefahren), and often the vowel in the stem changes (trinken, getrunken). You have to learn these forms by heart.

Most irregular verbs form the Perfekt with haben: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen. Verbs of movement or change of place (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen) and the verbs sein and bleiben use sein: Wir sind nach Rom geflogen. The forms of the verb are the same as for the regular ones, only the Partizip II is new.

A small group of mixed verbs has the regular ending -t but also changes its stem: bringen, gebracht. Learn them as a separate group. Verbs with a separable prefix put ge- in the middle: ankommen, angekommen; einsteigen, eingestiegen. The verb bekommen and the verb beginnen have no ge-: bekommen, begonnen.
intro.rule_summary: haben/sein + Partizip II at the end; irregular Partizip II usually ends in -en with a changed stem (gesehen, gefahren); movement verbs, sein and bleiben take sein.

intro.title: Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
explanation: The Perfekt has two parts: haben (or sein) in second position and the participle (Partizip II) at the end. Regular verbs form the participle as ge- + stem + -t: arbeiten → gearbeitet.
Separable verbs have a prefix such as an-, auf-, ein-, mit- or ab-. In the participle, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: anrufen → angerufen, aufräumen → aufgeräumt, einkaufen → eingekauft.
Inseparable verbs start with be-, ver-, er-, ent- or zer-. They get no ge- at all: besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, bekommen → bekommen.
Most verbs use haben. Verbs of movement or change of place or state, such as ankommen, aufstehen and mitkommen, use sein: Lena ist angekommen.

intro.title: Time expressions: am, um, im, seit, vor
explanation: German uses small words to say when something happens. Use am with days, dates and parts of the day (am Samstag, am 5. Mai, am Abend). Use um with clock times (um acht Uhr). Use im with months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
Use seit for something that started in the past and is still true now: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier. Use vor for something that happened a certain time ago: Die Party war vor einer Woche.

After seit and vor the next word changes: einem Jahr, einer Woche, zwei Tagen. Learn these as fixed chunks at A1: seit einem Jahr, seit einer Woche, vor einem Jahr, vor einer Woche, vor zwei Tagen. With a day or month there is no change: seit Montag, seit Juni.

intro.title: Prepositions with the accusative: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um
explanation: Some German prepositions are always followed by the accusative case. Five important ones are für (for), durch (through), ohne (without), gegen (against, into) and um (around). You never have to think about 'where' or 'whether something moves'; these five always take the accusative.
In the accusative only the masculine nouns change: der becomes den and ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural nouns look the same as in the nominative: die Lampe, das Bett, die Stühle.
After ohne you often use no article at all when you mean 'without any': ohne Kissen. If you want to say 'without the pillow', use ohne das Kissen.

intro.title: Two-way prepositions: Wo? or Wohin?
explanation: Some prepositions, like in, an, auf, vor, hinter and neben, can take the dative or the accusative. They are called two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen). The question decides the case.

Wo? asks about a place, with no change of place: Wo ist der Bus? You use the dative: Der Bus ist an der Haltestelle. Wohin? asks about a movement or a direction: Wohin fährst du? You use the accusative: Ich fahre in die Stadt.

Only the masculine and the neuter change between the two cases (der/das becomes dem for Wo?, den/das for Wohin?). The feminine is die for Wohin? and der for Wo?. Often in dem becomes im and an dem becomes am.

intro.title: Putting things somewhere or being somewhere: stellen/stehen, legen/liegen, hängen
explanation: German has two kinds of verbs for position. One kind is an action: you put something somewhere (Wohin?). The other kind is a state: something is somewhere (Wo?). stellen = to put upright, legen = to lay flat, hängen = to hang up. These answer Wohin? and use the accusative: Ich lege den Ausweis auf den Tisch.

The state verbs are stehen (upright), liegen (flat) and hängen (hanging). They answer Wo? and use the dative: Der Ausweis liegt auf dem Tisch. Note that hängen is used for both: Ich hänge die Jacke an den Haken (action). Die Jacke hängt am Haken (state).
The little words auf, an, in and neben change the case. Wohin? = accusative (den Tisch, die Tasche). Wo? = dative (dem Tisch, der Tasche). Learn the pairs as blocks: auf den Tisch / auf dem Tisch.
Do not mix up the verbs: legen and stellen need a person who does something (Ich lege ...). liegen and stehen just describe where something is (Der Pass liegt ...).
intro.rule_summary: Wohin? = stellen / legen / hängen + accusative; Wo? = stehen / liegen / hängen + dative.

intro.title: A1 review: the building blocks of simple German
explanation: In a German statement the verb is always in second position: Jonas wohnt in Berlin. If you put another word first, the verb stays second: In Berlin wohnt Jonas. In a W-question (wer, wo, woher, wie) the question word comes first and the verb second: Woher kommst du?

Regular verbs take endings that match the person: ich -e, du -st, er/sie -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. The two most important verbs, sein and haben, are irregular. Use sein for names, origin, feelings and age (Ich bin 25). Use haben for Hunger, Durst and things you own (Ich habe Durst).

Nouns have a gender (der, die, das) and a plural, so learn each noun with its article. Negate a noun with kein/keine (Ich habe keine Zeit) and everything else with nicht (Ich komme nicht aus Spanien). Use du with friends and family, and Sie (capital S) with adults you do not know well.
intro.rule_summary: Verb in second position, endings match the person, learn nouns with their article, kein for nouns, nicht for the rest, du for friends and Sie for formal situations.
